_**User**_

```3. Best way to keep kernel state: external kernel
If preserving variables/session is the real goal, make the kernel outlive VS Code’s Extension Host:

Start a Jupyter server outside VS Code (or use a remote/existing kernel)
In the notebook: Select Kernel → Existing Jupyter Server… (or an already-running kernel)
Install the VSIX / restart extensions
The server process keeps running; Jupyter reconnects. Local “start kernel for me” sessions usually do not survive EH restart cleanly.```
Add as a feature to my extension the ability to easily spawn/connect to/monitor external kernels using the same workflow as spawning an internal kernel

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The architecture uses the official Jupyter API. An external kernel would be launched as a detached child process with a known token and port. It would run under the user's configured Python path or system PATH.

A `JupyterServerProvider` and `JupyterServerCommandProvider` would register the external server collection. Users could launch or connect through commands or the kernel picker. A status bar and output channel would monitor the server PID, URL, HTTP health, and kernel idle/busy state.

Server metadata such as PID, port, token, and base URL would be persisted in globalState. On activation, the extension would re-attach to the existing process if it is still alive. Deactivation would not kill the server.

The durable server would appear in the kernel picker exactly like a local kernel. Users could select it, start a session, and pick a kernel without any extra steps.

Two design questions remain. Should the extension only manage one local durable server, or also support connecting to an existing remote URL? Should the control appear only in the kernel picker, or also as a toolbar button?

The extension will support spawning a local durable server and connecting to an existing remote URL. The server will integrate into the kernel picker via JupyterServerCollection. It will persist across Extension Host restarts. The server will run under the configured pythonPath. The server will not be killed when the extension stops. Users will need an explicit command to stop it.

Windows spawn details are being considered. The server will run from the workspace folder. The concrete plan is to ask two scope questions before creating the implementation plan.

The design now favors one durable server per workspace folder, or global if no folder exists. The primary workflow follows internal kernels: users select the server from the kernel picker and start a session. A status bar and command palette will handle monitoring, starting, stopping, and reconnecting. Connecting to an existing remote URL will be a secondary command that registers a URL into the collection.

The user wants the extension to spawn the Jupyter server itself rather than just registering an external connection. I am now checking the extension.ts file to determine where to wire up the startup logic.
</details></think>

Microsoft's jupyter-server-provider-sample starts Jupyter in the terminal, which dies with the Extension Host. A detached process is needed instead so the kernel survives EH restarts.

The kernel picker will be the primary workflow, with dedicated start, stop, and status bar commands as a secondary layer. Detached servers will be spawned with a known token, persisted in globalState, and rehydrated on activation. Health checks and status bars will monitor both server and kernel status. Users can also paste existing server URLs into the collection.

A concrete module layout is planned under `src/externalKernel/` with separate files for server management, collection wiring, status bar monitoring, and startup logic. Dedicated commands will handle starting, stopping, connecting existing servers, showing status, copying URLs, and optionally opening the kernel picker.

The implementation will reuse the existing Python path setting and support a configurable preferred port. Auto-start on notebook open will likely be disabled by default. Detached processes will run with hidden windows and ignored standard input, while output pipes to capture the server URL from stdout.

On activation, the extension will probe each saved server’s `/api/status` endpoint with its token. Live servers get re-registered into the collection; dead ones get cleared from globalState.

The status bar will display a server icon followed by the server address and current status—idle, busy, or down.

To keep server logs accessible after the process detaches, stdout and stderr will be redirected into a log file inside the extension’s globalStorage directory. This avoids losing output when stdio is ignored.

The extension will persist server PIDs so the Stop command can kill the process directly, while deactivation never terminates running servers. The kernel picker will auto-start a durable server when selected if none is running, then return connection info so users pick a Python kernel exactly as they would with a remote server. A command-palette Start option will also let users pre-warm a server before selecting a kernel.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
VS Code cannot be required outside the extension host. I will test the parse and probe logic through a quick self-check, or simply verify TypeScript compilation and review the code carefully.

Cancellation errors during connect are handled correctly. Error messages for failed connectExisting will bubble to Jupyter. The status bar hides when no servers are running, but the toolbar button still allows starting a kernel. The plan specifies polling while a notebook is open or a durable server is registered, and the toolbar provides the entry point.

A failed initial spawn may leave an orphaned Jupyter process if kill fails. A timeout on the first attempt risks port conflicts with the fallback server; a fresh port would prevent this. The ChildProcess type was removed. Prompting returns undefined on back and throws CancellationError on escape, which correctly propagates to handleCommand.

Empty-string acceptance keeps the prompt visible. OutputChannel is registered once via subscription and disposed correctly. Extension deactivation disposes the collection but leaves the underlying process running. I am also checking the JupyterServer type and resolveJupyterServer return type.

Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500
$deadProbe = $true
try { Invoke-WebRequest -Uri &#34;$base/api/status?token=$token&#34; -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 2 | Out-Null; $deadProbe = $false } catch { $deadProbe = $true }
Write-Host &#34;after_stop_unreachable=$deadProbe&#34;

```bash
$py = (Resolve-Path .\.tmp-durable-venv\Scripts\python.exe).Path
$log = Join-Path $env:TEMP "durable-smoke.log"
$token = -join ((1..48) | ForEach-Object { '{0:x}' -f (Get-Random -Max 16) })
# pick free port
$listener = [System.Net.Sockets.TcpListener]::new([System.Net.IPAddress]::Loopback, 0)
$listener.Start(); $port = $listener.LocalEndpoint.Port; $listener.Stop()
$base = "http://127.0.0.1:$port"
Write-Host "Starting on $base token=$token"
$proc = Start-Process -FilePath $py -ArgumentList @('-m','jupyter_server','--no-browser',"--port=$port","--ServerApp.token=$token","--ServerApp.password=") -PassThru -WindowStyle Hidden -RedirectStandardOutput $log -RedirectStandardError "$log.err"
Write-Host "pid $($proc.Id)"
$ok = $false
for ($i=0; $i -lt 60; $i++) {
  try {
    $r = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$base/api/status?token=$token" -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 2
    if ($r.StatusCode -eq 200) { $ok = $true; break }
  } catch {}
  Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500
}
Write-Host "health=$ok"
# simulate EH restart: only probe by pid/url, don't keep process handle
$alive = -not $proc.HasExited
Write-Host "process_alive=$alive"
# stop like manager
taskkill /PID $proc.Id /T /F 2>$null | Out-Null
Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500
$deadProbe = $true
try { Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$base/api/status?token=$token" -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 2 | Out-Null; $deadProbe = $false } catch { $deadProbe = $true }
Write-Host "after_stop_unreachable=$deadProbe"
if ($ok -and $alive -and $deadProbe) { Write-Host "SMOKE_PASS"; exit 0 } else { Write-Host "SMOKE_FAIL"; exit 1 }
```

_**Agent (default)**_

Durable external Jupyter kernels are implemented and compile cleanly.

### What you get
- **Spawn** a detached local Jupyter server (`python -m jupyter notebook`, fallback `jupyter_server`) that survives Extension Host restart
- **Kernel Picker** entry: **Durable Jupyter (survives reload)** with Start / Connect URL
- **Monitor** via status bar + **Durable Jupyter** output channel
- **Stop** only kills servers this extension spawned (connected URLs are unregister-only)

### Files
- [`src/externalKernel/DurableServerManager.ts`](src/externalKernel/DurableServerManager.ts)
- [`src/externalKernel/jupyterServerCollection.ts`](src/externalKernel/jupyterServerCollection.ts)
- [`src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts`](src/externalKernel/statusMonitor.ts)
- [`src/externalKernel/startup.ts`](src/externalKernel/startup.ts)
- Wired in [`src/extension.ts`](src/extension.ts) + [`package.json`](package.json)

### Commands (category **Durable Jupyter**)
`start` · `stop` · `connect` · `copyUrl` · `showLog` · `selectKernel` (toolbar) · status-bar menu

### Settings
- `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.defaultPort` (`0` = auto)
- `jupyter-cell-tags.externalKernel.autoRegisterOnNotebookOpen`
- Uses `jupyterEnhancements.kernel.pythonPath` for the Python that launches the server

### How to use
1. Set `jupyterEnhancements.kernel.pythonPath` to an env with Jupyter installed
2. Open a notebook → **Select Kernel → Durable Jupyter (survives reload) → Start Durable Server**
3. Pick a kernel, run `x = 1`
4. **Developer: Restart Extension Host** → reconnect to Durable Jupyter → `x` should still exist

Verified: TypeScript compile + spawn/health/stop smoke test against a temp `jupyter_server` venv. Full EH-reconnect with your `jlab` env needs a run in the Extension Development Host.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The CLI window likely appears because `detached: true` creates its own console on Windows, and `windowsHide` does not work properly with detached processes. Additionally, `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` is ignored when combined with `DETACHED_PROCESS`.

The disappearing window means the process is dying immediately, not just flashing. This points to two separate issues: the console flash from detached mode, and the process exiting right away.

The immediate exit likely stems from missing Jupyter, a password argument parsing bug on Windows, or a Python stub issue. Without detached mode, the process may still die during Electron Host restarts unless it is placed in a separate job object. Using `cmd /c start /b` could hide the console but is messy.

Using `pythonw.exe` instead of `python.exe` would eliminate the console window entirely. Another option is combining `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` with `DETACHED_PROCESS` flags. The best approach depends on whether the process must survive Electron Host restarts or simply run silently. Microsoft Jupyter samples launch in a terminal, so their pattern differs from hiding the console.

A preflight check should verify that `jupyter_server` is installed before spawning the process. Empty password arguments such as `--NotebookApp.password=` may cause argparse to fail on Windows. Inheriting file descriptors through detached mode can also break pipe connections once the parent closes them.

Prefer `pythonw.exe` as the executable sibling when available. Use `creationflags: CREATE_NO_WINDOW | CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` paired with `detached: true`, or apply `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` alone without detached and rely on process independence to survive Electron Host restarts. Redirecting logs through file paths opened by the child, or using a `.bat` wrapper with `pythonw`, avoids broken pipe issues. Node.js is the recommended approach for Windows console hiding and process persistence.

Use `windowsHide` with piped or ignored standard input/output streams. Modern Jupyter Server accepts `--IdentityProvider.token` or `--ServerApp.token` instead of the legacy empty password flag. `execFile` with `shell: false` is preferable. The concrete plan resolves to `pythonw.exe` on Windows when it is present alongside `python.exe`.

Detached mode should be avoided because `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` is ignored when combined with `DETACHED_PROCESS`. The better approach is `detached: false` with `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` and `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP`, then unref the child. On Windows, unref’d children usually survive parent death unless a Job Object is configured to kill them. Electron’s Extension Host may kill spawned processes during restarts, so true survival requires detaching the process from the host’s job object.

Preflight checks should import `jupyter_server` directly rather than `notebook`, and surface the log tail in the error message when spawning fails. On Windows, use `--ServerApp.token` and `--ServerApp.open_browser=False` instead of legacy empty password flags. To avoid broken pipe issues, spawn with `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']` and redirect Jupyter output to a log file via shell redirection.

Opening the log file synchronously with `fs.openSync` and passing the raw file descriptor to `spawn` should ensure the child inherits the handle on Windows. The existing async `fs.open` approach should also work if Node marks the descriptor as inheritable. If the spawn fails, the error notification should include the last N lines of the log so the user can see messages like "No module named jupyter". The user should also be asked whether their Python installation comes from the Windows Store, since that often causes silent failures.
</details></think>

Windows executable selection\n\nAfter resolving a runnable interpreter:\n\n- If path ends with `python.exe` and sibling `pythonw.exe` exists, **spawn with `pythonw.exe`** (window subsystem → no console).\n- Still use that env’s site-packages (same directory layout).\n- Reject / skip Microsoft Store alias paths under `WindowsApps\\python.exe` during candidate checks (they flash and are not real envs).\n\n### 2. Preflight Jupyter before spawn\n\nRun (hidden, short timeout):\n\n`python -c \"import jupyter_server\"` → else `import notebook`\n\nIf both fail, throw immediately:\n\n`Python at X has no Jupyter. Install jupyter_server in that env, or set jupyter-cell-tags.jupyterEnhancements.kernel.pythonPath to an env that already has it.`\n\nDo not attempt a 60s wait when the module is missing.\n\n### 3. Reliable Windows spawn + fail-fast exit watch\n\nIn `doStartManaged`:\n\n- Prefer **`jupyter_server` first**, then `jupyter notebook` fallback.\n- Drop empty `--NotebookApp.password=` / `--ServerApp.password=` flags (can confuse Windows argv parsing). Keep token + `--no-browser` / `ServerApp.open_browser=False`.\n- Open log with `fs.openSync(logPath, 'a')` and pass that fd for stdout/stderr (reliable inheritance).\n- Spawn options: `{ detached: true, windowsHide: true, stdio: ['ignore', out, out], shell: false }`.\n- **Do not `unref()` until ready or failed.** Attach `child.on('exit')` so if the process dies during wait, fail immediately with exit code + **last ~40 lines of the log file** in the error (and Output channel).\n- Only then `unref()` so the server outlives EH.\n\n### 4. User-visible failure\n\nIf start fails, show the log-tail error in the existing notification/warning paths (`start` command / `selectKernel` auto-start). Offer **Show Durable Jupyter Log** so the flash is diagnosable without digging in globalStorage.\n\n## Verification\n\n1. Point `pythonPath` at an env **with** `jupyter_server` → Start Durable: no console flash (or negligible), status bar shows `Durable :port`, `/api/status` OK.\n2. Point at an env **without** Jupyter → immediate clear error (no 60s hang, no mysterious flash-only failure).\n3. After successful start: Restart Extension Host → server still up (rehydrate), notebook can reconnect via Durable collection.\n4. Stop still kills only the managed PID via `taskkill /T /F`.\n",

_**Agent (default)**_

Yes — that message was the old behavior, and the Windows fix addresses it for the usual failure mode.

Previously the child crashed right away (flashing console), but we still polled `/api/status` for up to 60s, then showed “Timed out waiting for jupyter_server…”.

Now:
1. **Preflight** — if that Python can’t `import jupyter_server` / `notebook`, you get an immediate clear error (no 60s wait)
2. **Exit watch** — if the process dies during start, we fail right away with the log tail instead of waiting out the timeout
3. **Show Log** on the error/warning so you can see why

A timeout can still appear only if Jupyter stays alive but never becomes reachable — uncommon compared to the flash-and-die case you hit.

_**Agent (default)**_

Unlikely to be Durable Kernel. **Execute Cell Group** goes through `notebook.cell.execute`, and **Jupyter Enhancements** (on by default) hijacks that command in a way that only runs one cell.

### What Execute Cell Group does

[`executeGroup`](src/notebookRunGroups/util/cellActionHelpers.ts) collects every cell with the chosen tag and calls:

```143:143:src/notebookRunGroups/util/cellActionHelpers.ts
    vscode.commands.executeCommand('notebook.cell.execute', { ranges: targetCells });
```

with **all** matching ranges.

### What breaks it

With `jupyter-cell-tags.features.jupyterEnhancements` enabled (default `true`), [`registerHijacks`](src/jupyterEnhancements/extension.ts) replaces `notebook.cell.execute` with `runSingleHandler`, which only uses the **first** range:

```298:300:src/jupyterEnhancements/extension.ts
	else if (args && args.ranges && args.ranges.length > 0) {
		cell = editor.notebook.cellAt(args.ranges[0].start);
	}
```

So the group “runs,” but only the first tagged cell executes — which feels like unreliable Execute Cell Group.

Durable Kernel doesn’t touch `notebook.cell.execute` or run-group registration; it only adds server/collection/status-bar commands.

### How to confirm

1. Temporarily disable **Jupyter Cell Tags → Features → Jupyter Enhancements**, reload, retry Execute Cell Group.
2. Or watch the **Jupyter Enhancements** output for `[DEBUG] >> Hijack: Run Single` / `[Single] Executing Cell Index: …` when you run a group.

### Secondary quirks (pre-existing)

- `executeGroup` doesn’t pass `document` / `notebookUri` (only `ranges`), so native execute can be flaky without a focused notebook.
- Toolbar invoke often has no cell context (`argNotebookCell` returns undefined), so it relies on the active notebook editor.

### Fix direction (when you want Agent mode)

In the hijack: if `args.ranges.length > 1`, forward all ranges through `withNativeCellExecute` (or run them sequentially like `runSequenceHandler`) instead of only `ranges[0]`. Optionally have `executeGroup` pass `{ document: doc.uri, ranges: targetCells }`.
